title: El Nino nears historic peak as Pacific warming raises global weather extremes
html:
Models predict the tropical Pacific warming to peak in December or January and remain above El Niño thresholds through to autumn 2027 (March-May). | Photo Credit: MUSTAFAH KK

A strong-to-very strong El Nino is currently developing. The weekly relative Niño3.4 index was +2.67°C for the week ending 22 November 2026, down from its peak value for the event so far (+2.88°C).

This event is on track to be one of the strongest El Nino events on record, but it has not yet reached the highest monthly value on record (since 1900) during the 1982–83 El Niño, according to the Southern Hemisphere monitoring report of the Bureau of Meteorology, Australia.

The weekly relative Niño3.4 index was +2.67°C for the week ending 22 November 2026, down from its peak value for the event so far (+2.88°C) | Photo Credit: Bureau of Meteorology, Australia

Atmospheric indicators continue to be consistent with a strong El Nino, including weakened or reversed trade winds, enhanced cloudiness in the central to eastern tropical Pacific, and reduced cloud over the Maritime Continent.

The 30-day Southern Oscillation Index value as of 22 November has increased to –7.8, consistent with seasonal variability in tropical activity.

Most models, including the bureau’s, predict the tropical Pacific warming to peak in December or January and remain above El Niño thresholds through to autumn 2027 (March-May).

Relative Niño3.4 values are forecast to equal or surpass the highest values observed since reliable records began in 1950.

There is an ongoing positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) event. The weekly IOD index is down to +0.53°C for the week ending 22 November 2026.

The positive IOD is forecast to further weaken through November, returning to neutral by early summer (December). This is in line with all international models assessed and the typical IOD life cycle.

Sea surface temperature (SST) analysis for the week ending 22 November shows SSTs are up to 1.2°C above average around much of Australia’s south and northeast, increasing to up to 3°C above average in the southeast. SSTs west of Australia are near average.

SSTs are at record levels globally. October 2026 was the warmest October on record, 1.00°C above the 1961-1990 average. Since June, monthly global-averaged SSTs have been the warmest on record for each month.

Sea surface temperatures are expected to warm over the coming months across much of the Australian region, particularly in Australia’s north and in the Coral Sea.

Warmer waters can boost the risk of marine heatwaves and increase atmospheric moisture and energy, which can fuel storms and rain systems, increasing the potential for high-intensity rainfall.

The Southern Annular Mode (SAM) index is positive as at 21 November and has remained above the positive threshold for most of November to date. It is expected to revert to neutral over the next week, the report added.

Published on November 24, 2026
summary: El Niño nears historic peak amid record global ocean warming and shifting Indian Ocean conditions, with forecasts for extended El Niño and rising extreme weather risks.
